title: First contact: read your dispatch
concept: This is a terminal: you type a command, press Enter, and Linux prints the result. Your first command is cat, which prints the contents of a text file to the screen. Reading a file with cat never changes it.
brief: Your home directory holds a file called dispatch.txt. Read it to find your first flag.

files.text: Welcome, operator. Your first dispatch contains {{FLAG}}

hints: The command is cat, a space, then the filename.
Run cat dispatch.txt, then highlight the CYBER{...} text in the output.
example: cat notes.txt      # prints everything inside notes.txt
explanation: Every command starts with its name, followed by any arguments, separated by spaces. Here, cat is the command and the filename is its argument. The text before the $ (user@cybercodex:~) is the prompt. It shows who you are and where you are, and you don't type it. The ~ means your home directory, which is where every mission starts unless it says otherwise.
pitfall: Don't type the $ or anything before it. That's the prompt, not part of the command. And don't run the flag as a command: paste it into the flag box.
transfer: What would happen if you ran cat dispatch.txt twice? Would the file change?
steps: Type cat dispatch.txt and press Enter.
Find the flag in the output. It looks like CYBER{...}.
Highlight the whole flag with your mouse (it copies automatically) and paste it into the flag box.
why: Security work starts with reading: config files, logs, notes left on a system. cat is the quickest way to look inside a file.

title: Know your operator
concept: Linux always knows which user is running each command. whoami prints your username, and id adds your numeric user ID (UID) and the groups you belong to.
brief: Find out who you are, then collect the dispatch addressed to you.
hints: whoami and id don't need any arguments.
Read the dispatch with cat /home/user/operator.txt.
example:
whoami      # prints your username
id          # prints your UID, GID and groups
explanation: Your username is the human-friendly name. The UID is the number Linux actually uses to decide what you may read or change. Groups give extra access to shared files. This lab has one practice user, user, so nothing you do here touches your real computer or anyone else's environment.
pitfall: The user shown in the lab isn't your CyberCodex account or email. It's the practice user inside your environment.
transfer: How is a username different from a UID, and why would Linux use the number?
steps: Run whoami and note the username.
Run id to see your UID and groups.
Read your dispatch with cat /home/user/operator.txt.
why: On any system you break into or defend, the first question is "who am I running as?". Your user decides what you can access.

title: Your place in the tree
concept: pwd (print working directory) shows exactly where you are in the filesystem, as a full path that starts with /.
brief: Confirm where you are, then read the coordinates file stored there.
hints: pwd needs no arguments.
You start in /home/user, and coordinates.txt is right there.
example:
pwd         # prints something like /home/user
ls          # lists what's in that directory
explanation: The Linux filesystem is one big tree. The very top is the root, written as /. Your home directory, /home/user, is a branch of that tree. Whenever you type a filename without a leading /, Linux looks for it in the directory pwd shows. That's why the same command can work in one place and fail in another.
pitfall: A path tells you where something lives. coordinates.txt here and /coordinates.txt at the root would be two different files.
transfer: Why might cat notes.txt work in one directory but fail in another?
steps: Run pwd to see your current directory.
Run ls to see what's in it.
Read coordinates.txt with cat.
why: When a command says "No such file", checking pwd is the first thing to do. Most of the time you're simply in the wrong place.

title: The dispatch shelf
concept: ls lists the files in a directory. Files whose names start with a dot (like .config) are hidden from a normal listing. ls -a shows everything, and ls -l shows details like permissions and size.
brief: Something is hidden in your home directory. List everything, find the hidden dispatch and read it.

files.text: Not all files appear in a normal listing.

hints: Try ls -a.
The hidden file is called .dispatch. Run cat .dispatch.
example:
ls          # normal listing
ls -a       # include hidden files (names starting with .)
ls -l       # long listing with permissions and sizes
explanation: Options such as -a and -l change how a command behaves. Hidden files are just a naming convention to reduce clutter, not a security feature: anyone who knows the name, and has permission, can read them. Remember that filenames are case sensitive, so Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files.
pitfall: The dot is part of the filename, so cat dispatch won't work. Listing a file also doesn't show its contents; you still need cat.
transfer: Does hiding a file with a dot stop another user from reading it?
steps: Run ls and notice that only readme.txt appears.
Run ls -a to reveal hidden files.
Read the hidden file with cat (keep the dot in its name).
why: Attackers and admins both stash things in dotfiles. Always use ls -a when you're exploring a system.

title: Walk to the relay
concept: cd (change directory) moves you to another directory. cd .. goes up one level, cd - jumps back to where you just were, and plain cd takes you home.
brief: Walk into the stations/relay directory, read the message waiting there, then head back home.
hints: Run ls to see the stations directory.
From home, cd stations/relay takes you straight there.
example:
cd /tmp     # go to /tmp
pwd         # confirm where you are
cd -        # jump back to the previous directory
explanation: Your terminal remembers one current directory. After a cd, every filename you type is looked up from the new location. Directories inside directories are written with / between them, so stations/relay means "the relay folder inside stations". Use pwd or ls after moving if you want to check where you landed.
pitfall: cd doesn't print anything when it works. No output means success, so run pwd if you want to check.
transfer: What's the difference between cd .. and cd /?
steps: Run cd stations/relay (Tab can complete the names for you).
Run cat message.txt to read the flag.
Run cd on its own to return home.
why: Moving around the filesystem quickly is the core skill for every later mission and every real system you'll work on.

title: Read without moving
concept: An absolute path starts with / and points to the same place no matter where you are. You can read a file anywhere by giving cat its absolute path, without moving.
brief: A dispatch is waiting in /opt/academy. Read it without leaving your home directory.
hints: Start the path with /.
Run cat /opt/academy/dispatch.txt.
example: cat /etc/hostname      # read a file by its absolute path
explanation: So far you've used relative paths, which start from your current directory. Absolute paths start from the root /. They're handy in instructions and scripts because they always work, whatever directory the terminal happens to be in.
pitfall: The leading slash matters. opt/academy/dispatch.txt (no slash) would look inside your current directory instead.
transfer: How could you read a file in another directory without going into it?
steps: Stay in your home directory (no cd needed).
Run cat /opt/academy/dispatch.txt.
Optional: run pwd to confirm you never moved.
why: Logs and config files live in fixed places like /var/log and /etc. Reading them by absolute path is something you'll do constantly.

title: Ask the manual
concept: You don't have to memorize every command. man COMMAND opens a command's manual, and help lists every command this lab supports.
brief: Use the manual for ls to learn how to show hidden files, then use that to find the hidden receipt in /opt/academy/helpdesk.
hints: man ls shows that -a includes hidden entries.
Run ls -a /opt/academy/helpdesk, then cat /opt/academy/helpdesk/.receipt.
example:
help        # list every supported command
man cat     # read the manual for cat
explanation: Real professionals look things up constantly. Read a manual's first line to see the basic syntax, then try one option at a time. This lab's manuals describe its supported subset; on a full Linux system, man pages are longer and cover more options.
pitfall: Not every command or option you see online exists here. If one isn't supported, the lab will tell you, so check man first.
transfer: How would you check whether an option is supported before using it?
steps: Run man ls and look for the option that shows hidden entries.
List /opt/academy/helpdesk with that option.
Read the hidden file by its full path.
why: Knowing how to find the answer is more valuable than memorizing it. Every tool you meet later will come with a manual.

title: One floor up
concept: A relative path can climb up with .. before going back down. ../store/receipt.txt means "go up one level, enter store, then find receipt.txt".
brief: You're standing in the work directory. The receipt is in the store directory next door. Read it without using an absolute path.
hints: You're already in work, so there's no need to cd.
.. climbs out of work, then store/receipt.txt goes into the neighbouring folder.
example:
cat ../notes.txt          # a file one level above you
cat ./notes.txt           # a file right here (same as notes.txt)
explanation: This mission starts you inside /home/user/work. The . in a path means "here" and .. means "the parent directory", and they can appear anywhere in a path. If a path confuses you, resolve it one piece at a time: start at pwd, then apply each part in order.
pitfall: ../store is not /store. The first depends on where you are; the second always starts at the root.
transfer: Starting in /home/user/work, where does ../../ point to?
steps: Run pwd to confirm you're in /home/user/work.
Run ls .. to see the directories next to work.
Read the receipt with cat ../store/receipt.txt.
why: Relative paths keep commands short and portable. You'll see ../ in scripts, configs and exploits all the time.

title: Names with spaces
concept: The shell splits what you type into separate words at spaces. To use a filename that contains a space, wrap it in quotes so it stays one argument.
brief: Someone saved the shift notes with a space in the filename. Read shift notes.txt.
hints: Without quotes, cat thinks you gave it two filenames.
Put the whole name in quotes: cat "shift notes.txt".
example:
cat "my report.txt"      # one file whose name has a space
cat my report.txt        # two files: my and report.txt
explanation: Without quotes, cat shift notes.txt asks for two files: shift and notes.txt. Quotes keep the whole name together, and the shell removes them before cat sees the name. Double quotes and single quotes both work for this. Single quotes are completely literal, which matters once you meet variables.
pitfall: Tab completion can add a backslash before the space for you. That works too.
transfer: Why is cat "a b.txt" different from cat a b.txt?
steps: Run ls to see the filename.
Read it with cat "shift notes.txt" (including the quotes).
why: Real systems are full of awkward filenames, especially anything copied from Windows or macOS. Quoting correctly prevents some nasty mistakes.

title: Copy a field report
concept: cp copies a file and leaves the original where it is. mkdir creates a new directory. A copy needs its destination directory to exist first.
brief: Make a backup of the field report: create a backup directory and copy report.txt into it. Your flag appears in reward.txt once the backup is in place.
hints: Create the folder first with mkdir backup.
The backup must end up at /home/user/backup/report.txt.
example:
mkdir copies                      # create a folder
cp notes.txt copies/notes.txt     # copy a file into it
explanation: A copy is a completely separate file with the same contents, so changing one later won't affect the other. cp won't create missing directories for you, so make the folder first with mkdir. This mission checks your filesystem: once the backup exists with the right contents, a reward.txt file containing your flag appears in your home directory.
pitfall: Copying onto an existing file replaces its contents with no warning. Check the destination carefully.
transfer: When would you choose cp instead of mv?
steps: Run mkdir backup.
Run cp report.txt backup/report.txt.
Read the reward with cat reward.txt.
why: Backing up a file before you touch it is a habit that saves careers, especially when you're editing configs on a live system.

title: Rename the incoming report
concept: mv moves or renames a file. Unlike cp, the old name disappears, because it's the same file under a new path.
brief: The incoming report has been approved. Rename incoming.txt to approved.txt, keeping its contents, and collect your reward.
hints: Both files are in your home directory.
Run mv incoming.txt approved.txt.
example:
mv draft.txt final.txt       # rename a file
mv final.txt reports/        # move it into a folder
explanation: Renaming and moving are the same operation in Linux: you're changing the path used to reach the file. mv old.txt new.txt renames it, and mv file.txt folder/ moves it into a folder. Afterwards, check that the old name is gone. Once the rename is correct, reward.txt appears with your flag.
pitfall: If incoming.txt still exists afterwards, you copied the file instead of moving it.
transfer: How could you prove you moved a file rather than copied it?
steps: Run mv incoming.txt approved.txt.
Run ls to check that incoming.txt is gone.
Read the reward with cat reward.txt.
why: Renaming files is everyday admin work, and knowing the difference between moving and copying avoids lost or duplicated data.

title: Beginner checkpoint: locate the parcel
concept: Checkpoint time: no new commands, just everything from chapters 1 to 3 combined. Work methodically: get to the right place, look at everything there (including hidden files), then read what you find.
brief: A parcel has been hidden somewhere in /opt/academy/relay/archive. Find it and recover its flag.

files.text: The parcel is hidden, not missing.

hints: Hidden files need ls -a.
The parcel is called .parcel.
example:
cd /some/place     # go there
ls -a              # look at everything, hidden files included
explanation: Investigations go faster when you split them into steps. First, where am I and where do I need to be? Second, what's here, including hidden entries? Third, which file is the one I want? Read the output carefully and separate the flag from the prompt and the other text.
pitfall: Copy only the CYBER{...} flag, not the text around it. Flags from a reset environment no longer count.
transfer: Could you reach the same parcel with both a relative path and an absolute path?
steps: Move into /opt/academy/relay/archive.
List everything there, including hidden files.
Read the hidden parcel.
why: This is how real exploration works: navigate, enumerate, read. You'll repeat this loop on every machine you investigate.

title: Search the relay log
concept: grep selects lines matching a pattern. By default matching is case sensitive. grep -n adds line numbers, while -i ignores case.
brief: Find the line containing RECEIPT in /var/log/relay.log and extract its flag.

files.text:
boot ready
status ok
RECEIPT {{FLAG}}
status waiting

hints: Search for the marker rather than reading every line.
The flag is on the matching line.
explanation: Text logs are sequences of records, commonly one per line. grep reduces noise by selecting matching records. -n helps locate a match in the original file; -v reverses selection. This simulator supports literal text and optional start/end anchors, not the full GNU regular-expression language.
pitfall: Case matters unless you select -i. The search pattern and filename are separate arguments.
transfer: How would you display every line except those containing DEBUG?
steps: Find the line containing RECEIPT in /var/log/relay.log and extract its flag.

title: Locate a filename
concept: find walks a directory tree. -name matches an entry name, not its contents. Quote wildcard patterns so the shell does not expand them first.
brief: Find parcel.txt below /opt/academy and read it.
hints: Use find with a starting directory and -name.
Read the returned full path with cat.
explanation: find searches names and metadata in a directory tree; grep searches file contents. Choosing the starting directory controls the search scope. A quoted -name pattern is interpreted by find rather than expanded by the shell before find starts.
pitfall: A filename match does not mean the file contains the desired record. Inspect it after discovery.
transfer: When would you use find first and grep second?
steps: Find parcel.txt below /opt/academy and read it.

title: Inspect a batch with globbing
concept: An unquoted * expands to matching names within one path component. A question mark matches one character. Dotfiles are not matched unless the pattern explicitly begins with a dot.
brief: Read all .txt files inside batches to locate the receipt.
hints: The wildcard should remain unquoted for shell expansion.
cat can read multiple expanded filenames.
explanation: Globbing happens before a command runs. If three names match, the command receives three arguments. The wildcard is limited to a single directory component in this simulator. A pattern with no matches remains literal, so the command can report that no such file exists.
pitfall: Quoting the wildcard prevents shell expansion. Dotfiles require an explicit dot in the pattern.
transfer: What different sets of names do *.txt and ?.txt select?
steps: Read all .txt files inside batches to locate the receipt.

title: Select the last dispatch
concept: head reads the beginning of input and tail reads the end. -n sets a line count. These commands help inspect large files without flooding the terminal.
brief: Read only the last line of dispatches.txt.

files.text:
old one
old two
old three
{{FLAG}}

hints: Use tail for the end of a file.
Set the count to one with -n 1.
explanation: Reading a small slice helps you understand a file before processing it. head and tail preserve record order within the selected slice. Here -n accepts a nonnegative line count; live tail-follow mode is not part of the simulation.
pitfall: tail -n 1 selects one line, not one character.
transfer: Which command would you use to inspect a file header?
steps: Read only the last line of dispatches.txt.

title: Filter the signal
concept: A pipe sends one command’s standard output to the next command’s standard input. It does not turn that output into filenames.
brief: Filter stream.log down to the DELIVER line using a pipeline, then copy the flag.
hints: The left command reads; the right command filters.
Use cat stream.log | grep DELIVER.
explanation: Standard input is a data stream consumed by a command. Standard output is the stream it produces. A pipe joins these streams. The right side receives the left side’s output as data, not as command-line arguments, which is why cat sample.log | grep READY needs no filename for grep.
pitfall: Do not add a filename to the receiving command unless you intend it to read that file instead of the pipe.
transfer: Why is a pipe different from running two commands separated by a semicolon?
steps: Filter stream.log down to the DELIVER line using a pipeline, then copy the flag.

title: Write a report
concept: The > operator writes standard output to a file, replacing its contents. The shell handles redirection before running the command. Be careful when overwriting an existing file.
brief: Write exactly relay ready followed by a newline to status.txt.
hints: echo normally adds a newline.
Use a redirect after the quoted message.
explanation: Redirection belongs to the shell. With >, the destination is created or truncated before the command starts. This is why reading and writing the same file in one command can erase the input before it is read. Use a different output path for transformations.
pitfall: Avoid cat sample.txt > sample.txt. Use a separate temporary destination.
transfer: Why can > destroy data even when the command itself is only reading?
steps: Write exactly relay ready followed by a newline to status.txt.

title: Append without erasing
concept: The >> operator appends output. It preserves existing content, unlike >. A newline separates records in a text log.
brief: Append restored as a second line in status.log, keeping the first line.
hints: Use two greater-than signs.
The resulting lines should be offline and restored.
explanation: Appending makes a log grow without rewriting its earlier records. echo normally adds a newline, so appended records become separate lines. If earlier content lacks a final newline, the next text may run into it; inspect the resulting file when formatting matters.
pitfall: Using > instead of >> replaces the entire previous log.
transfer: How would the output differ if you appended the same record twice?
steps: Append restored as a second line in status.log, keeping the first line.

title: Separate repeated messages
concept: sort puts lines in order. uniq compares adjacent lines; -u prints only lines that occur once in each adjacent group. Sort first when duplicates may be separated.
brief: Find the only nonduplicated line in messages.txt.
hints: First bring identical lines together.
Pipe sort into uniq -u.
explanation: uniq acts on runs of equal adjacent lines. A file can contain duplicates far apart that uniq alone will not combine. Sorting first groups equal lines together. The -c option counts each adjacent group; -u keeps only groups with a single member.
pitfall: sort changes order. Do not use it when the original sequence carries meaning you must preserve.
transfer: Why does uniq without sort sometimes leave repeated values?
steps: Find the only nonduplicated line in messages.txt.

title: Extract a manifest field
concept: cut -d chooses a delimiter and -f chooses a one-based field. This simple delimiter tool is not a general CSV parser with quoted-field support.
brief: Extract field 3 of manifest.txt, separated by colons.
hints: Count fields starting at one.
Use colon as the delimiter.
explanation: Delimited records split a line into fields. cut numbers fields from one, so field two follows the first delimiter. This lab intentionally uses simple records with no escaped delimiters. For a more complex file format, use a parser appropriate to that format.
pitfall: If a delimiter appears inside a quoted value, this simple cut command still treats it as a delimiter.
transfer: What does field 1 mean when there is no delimiter on the line?
steps: Extract field 3 of manifest.txt, separated by colons.

title: Decode the shipment label
concept: base64 represents bytes with printable characters. Encoding is not encryption: anyone can decode it. -d reverses the encoding.
brief: Decode label.b64 to reveal the flag.
hints: Read the supported syntax with man base64.
Use its decoding option.
explanation: Base64 is a reversible representation useful for transporting bytes in text channels. Encoded data may include padding characters at the end. Decoding yields the original bytes; do not assume that encoded content is secret or safe merely because it looks unreadable.
pitfall: Copying only part of an encoded line can cause an invalid-input error.
transfer: Why should a password not be protected with base64 alone?
steps: Decode label.b64 to reveal the flag.

title: Recover read permission
concept: Permissions describe read, write, and execute rights. u+r adds the owner read bit without replacing other bits. The teaching shell acts as the owner of challenge files.
brief: Inspect sealed.txt, restore owner read permission, and read it.
hints: Permission denied is the intended starting state.
Use chmod u+r, then cat again.
explanation: Permission bits are grouped for owner, group, and others. r means read, w means write, and x means execute or traverse. This simulator models access as the owner; it does not provide multi-user operating-system permissions. Symbolic changes such as u+r are useful because they preserve unrelated bits.
pitfall: File readability and parent-directory traversal are separate requirements.
transfer: What is preserved when you add u+r rather than replace the mode with an octal value?
steps: Inspect sealed.txt, restore owner read permission, and read it.

title: Intermediate checkpoint: process a manifest
concept: A pipeline can combine selection, field extraction, and decoding. Inspect each stage separately if you are unsure what data it produces.
brief: Find the READY record in /var/log/manifest, extract its colon-separated payload, and decode that payload.
hints: Start by selecting READY.
Its second field is base64-encoded.
explanation: Complex pipelines are easier to debug incrementally. Run the first stage and inspect its output. Add a second stage and check the shape again. Decode only the payload, not the record label. If a stage outputs nothing, inspect that stage before adding more commands.
pitfall: Including the READY: prefix in the base64 decoder input will not produce the intended message.
transfer: Which intermediate output would you inspect first if decoding failed?
steps: Find the READY record in /var/log/manifest, extract its colon-separated payload, and decode that payload.

title: Read through standard input
concept: The < operator connects a file to a command’s standard input. The command does not need to receive that filename as an argument.
brief: Decode the receipt using base64 with input redirection.
hints: Use < before the filename.
The decoding command remains base64 -d.
explanation: Input redirection gives a command an already-open input stream. It is useful for tools that naturally read standard input. It differs from passing a filename: the command sees the stream rather than using an operand to choose the source. Here both forms can achieve the same count.
pitfall: The arrow points from the file into the command. > points output toward a destination file.
transfer: Can you explain the data flow of wc -l < sample.log > count.txt?
steps: Decode the receipt using base64 with input redirection.

title: Keep a copy of the evidence
concept: tee copies standard input both to standard output and to a file. It is useful when you want to inspect an intermediate pipeline result and retain it.
brief: Filter the OK line from source.log and save exactly that line to evidence.txt.

files.text:
NO pending
OK relay restored
NO retry

hints: Pipe the filtered line into tee.
evidence.txt must contain only OK relay restored and its newline.
explanation: tee is named after a pipe junction: data continues to the terminal or next pipeline stage and is also written to a file. By default that file is replaced; -a appends. It helps preserve evidence while you inspect it.
pitfall: tee does not filter the input. Perform selection before tee if you only want selected records saved.
transfer: Where would you place tee to inspect the output of a middle pipeline stage?
steps: Filter the OK line from source.log and save exactly that line to evidence.txt.

title: Spot a changed line
concept: diff compares file content and reports differences. A difference gives it a nonzero exit status even though comparison worked; this is not the same as a runtime failure.
brief: Compare before.txt and after.txt and recover the newly added flag.
hints: The > marker identifies lines from the second file in this simulator.
Copy only the CYBER{...} text, without the diff marker.
explanation: Comparison is useful when a configuration or report has changed. This lab shows first-file lines with < and second-file lines with >; it does not implement GNU diff’s full patch format. A status of one means differences were found, so conditional commands need to account for that.
pitfall: Do not include the diff marker when copying a recovered value.
transfer: Why might diff first.txt second.txt && echo identical be useful?
steps: Compare before.txt and after.txt and recover the newly added flag.

title: Undo a reversed transmission
concept: rev reverses characters within each line. It does not reverse the order of lines. Combine simple transforms by reasoning about how data was changed.
brief: Reverse the characters of reversed.txt to recover the flag.
hints: Inspect man rev if needed.
Pass reversed.txt as the input file.
explanation: A transformation may change ordering within records or ordering among records. rev only reverses characters inside each line. If a message was reversed before encoding, undo those operations in reverse order to recover the original data.
pitfall: rev does not reverse the entire file as one character sequence.
transfer: If a value was reversed and then base64-encoded, which operation should you undo first?
steps: Reverse the characters of reversed.txt to recover the flag.

title: Store the route
concept: export sets a shell variable; $NAME expands its value in a later command. Single quotes preserve literal dollar signs, whereas double quotes permit expansion.
brief: Set DEST to /opt/academy/signal, then use "$DEST/receipt" to read the flag.
hints: Set the variable in one command and use it in the next.
Double-quote the expanded path.
explanation: Variables let you name a reusable value. Referencing $PLACE expands that value in a later command. This teaching shell keeps HOME, USER, and PATH fixed and does not implement full shell scoping or word splitting. Use a separate command after export before using the new variable.
pitfall: Single quotes around $PLACE print its name literally.
transfer: Why are quotes useful around expanded paths that may contain spaces?
steps: Set DEST to /opt/academy/signal, then use "$DEST/receipt" to read the flag.

title: Traverse a locked directory
concept: Execute permission on a directory controls traversal. Read permission permits listing names; these are distinct. A readable file cannot be reached through a directory you cannot traverse.
brief: Restore owner traversal on vault, then read vault/receipt.
hints: Inspect vault with stat.
The missing directory bit is x, not r.
explanation: Directory x allows walking through a path component. Directory r allows listing entry names. On a real system, a directory can allow traversal without allowing a listing. This lab models owner permissions so you can observe the difference without changing your actual system.
pitfall: Adding read permission to a file does not fix a missing traversal bit on its parent directory.
transfer: Why can a readable file still return permission denied?
steps: Restore owner traversal on vault, then read vault/receipt.

title: Recover after a failed check
concept: && runs the next command only after success. || runs it only after failure. test checks a condition and communicates through its exit status rather than printed text.
brief: Use test and || to create restored.txt containing recovered when missing.txt does not exist.
hints: A missing file makes test return a nonzero status.
The recovery branch goes after ||.
explanation: Commands communicate success with zero and other outcomes with nonzero status. && and || make later commands conditional on that status. test often prints nothing; silence is normal. The lab supports a small documented test subset rather than the whole shell expression language.
pitfall: Do not judge success only by whether output was printed.
transfer: Which branch executes when test -f missing.txt is false?
steps: Use test and || to create restored.txt containing recovered when missing.txt does not exist.

title: Count accepted records
concept: wc -l counts newline characters. A pipeline can filter records first and then count only the accepted set. A final line without a newline changes that count.
brief: Count lines containing ACCEPT in traffic.txt and write the count to count.txt.

files.text:
ACCEPT a
DROP b
ACCEPT c
ACCEPT d

hints: Filter before counting.
The expected count is three.
explanation: Counting meaningful records begins with deciding what qualifies as a match. After filtering, wc -l counts newline characters. The lab returns a plain count so it can be stored or used as evidence. Real utilities may add a filename label when given a filename operand.
pitfall: A file containing text without a final newline may have fewer newline characters than visible text records.
transfer: Why is filtering before counting different from counting the entire file?
steps: Count lines containing ACCEPT in traffic.txt and write the count to count.txt.

title: Normalize a status stream
concept: tr translates characters from its first set to its second. Unlike a word replacement tool, it maps individual characters. Uppercase and lowercase ranges are supported here.
brief: Translate status.txt to lowercase and save it as normalized.txt.
solution: cat status.txt | tr A-Z a-z > normalized.txt
hints: tr reads the pipeline, not a filename argument.
Map A-Z to a-z.
explanation: Character translation is a useful normalization step before comparisons or aggregation. tr operates on individual characters, not whole words. The simulator supports literal sets and a few explicit ranges; more elaborate character classes require a fuller environment.
pitfall: Passing a filename to tr does not make it read that file. Redirect or pipe the contents instead.
transfer: When would changing case lose information that should be preserved?
steps: Translate status.txt to lowercase and save it as normalized.txt.

title: Order numeric priorities
concept: Lexical sorting compares characters, so 10 can appear before 2. sort -n compares numeric values. head then selects the highest-priority item if smaller numbers mean earlier service.
brief: Sort priorities.txt numerically and save the smallest value to first.txt.
hints: Use numeric sorting before taking the first line.
The smallest value is 2.
explanation: Numbers stored as text can be sorted numerically or lexically. Choose based on what the data represents. Numeric sorting is appropriate for counts and priorities, while lexical sorting may be appropriate for identifiers. Once ordered, select a small slice for inspection.
pitfall: A value that starts with digits is not always semantically a number; a postal code, for example, is an identifier.
transfer: Why can lexical ordering put 10 before 2?
steps: Sort priorities.txt numerically and save the smallest value to first.txt.

title: Clean the staging folder
concept: rm removes files; rmdir removes an empty directory. In a real shell deletion is not a recycle-bin operation. Inspect exact paths before removing anything.
brief: Remove the two temporary files in staging, then remove the empty staging directory. Preserve keep.txt.
hints: List staging before deleting its contents.
Use rmdir only when staging is empty.
example:
ls scratch
rm scratch/example.tmp
rmdir scratch
explanation: Cleanup is a good place to prefer precise commands. Inspect the directory before deleting, remove only the intended entries, then use rmdir as a check that nothing remains. A simulator reset can restore these fixtures, but real Linux deletion often cannot be undone.
pitfall: A broad wildcard can match more files than intended. Never use deletion commands without understanding the target path.
transfer: Why is rmdir safer than recursive removal when you expect an empty directory?
steps: Remove the two temporary files in staging, then remove the empty staging directory. Preserve keep.txt.

title: Advanced checkpoint: restore the relay
concept: Combine discovery, filtering, decoding, and evidence preservation. Verify each stage rather than guessing a long command. There can be more than one correct sequence of commands.
brief: Locate dispatch.dat under /opt/academy, select the RELEASE record, decode its second colon-delimited field, and save the decoded flag in /home/user/final.txt. Submit that flag.
hints: Use find to locate the data before processing it.
Filter RELEASE, extract field 2, decode, and tee into final.txt.
explanation: A capstone brings discovery and transformation together. Keep an evidence trail: know where the source came from, what each pipeline stage changes, and where the final result is saved. Equivalent valid command sequences are accepted because the result matters more than one memorized solution.
pitfall: The final flag must also be saved at the requested path before the mission is complete.
transfer: How would you debug this workflow if you found the file but produced an empty final report?
steps: Locate dispatch.dat under /opt/academy, select the RELEASE record, decode its second colon-delimited field, and save the decoded flag in /home/user/final.txt. Submit that flag.
